title: The Heart's Own Current and the Pacemaker
topic: cardiac conduction and the artificial pacemaker
paragraphs: A heart lifted out of the body, kept warm and oxygenated, goes on beating with no brain attached.
That observation contains the whole subject.
The signal behind each beat is manufactured inside the heart, by a small population of cells that behave nothing like the muscle around them.
Every cardiac device ever built stands in for that internal source.
Ordinary working muscle cells are electrically patient.
Each holds a steady negative voltage and waits for a neighbor's wave of charge to shove it past threshold.
Such cells make an excellent relay and a hopeless starter.
Pacemaker cells never settle.
Their membranes are leaky in a particular way: the moment one reaches its most negative point, channels swing open that admit a slow trickle of positive charge, and the cell starts climbing again.
At roughly minus forty millivolts the cell fires, its upstroke carried mostly by calcium rather than by the fast sodium rush that drives working muscle.
Then it falls back and begins again.
Several tissues do this at different speeds.
The sinoatrial node, in the wall of the right atrium, drifts to threshold sixty to one hundred times a minute.
The atrioventricular junction manages forty to sixty.
The Purkinje fibers in the ventricular walls are slower still, twenty to forty.
Since all of them are excitable, the fastest wins: its wave resets the others before they finish.
The node leads by speed alone, not by rank, and the slower sites wait underneath as backups.
The wave leaving the node spreads across both atria, then meets a wall.
A ring of fibrous tissue separates atria from ventricles and carries no current.
One door leads through it, the atrioventricular node, low in the right atrium.
Beyond that door the signal enters the bundle of His, splits into two bundle branches, and fans through the Purkinje network, which hands it to ventricular muscle near the apex.
The ventricles therefore contract from the bottom upward, wringing blood toward the great vessels.
At the door the signal slows.
Conduction through the atrioventricular node takes about a tenth of a second, and the slowness is built in.
Its cells are thin, they are joined by comparatively few of the protein channels that pass current from cell to cell, and their upstroke depends on calcium.
The pause buys the ventricles their last measure of filling.
The delay does a second job that is easy to overlook.
It rations.
Flutter runs the atria at about three hundred impulses a minute, and fibrillation is faster still, with no order at all.
The ventricles cannot follow either rhythm and survive, and nothing in the ventricles is equipped to refuse.
The node refuses on their behalf, passing only a fraction.
A narrow, slow, easily exhausted passage is poor design for speed and excellent design for protection.
The most conspicuous bottleneck in the system is also its finest safety feature.
When conduction along that route falters, clinicians call it a block, and the word misleads anyone who hears it as a plug in a pipe.
Nothing is obstructed.
A block is a failure of the signal to arrive, late or not at all, at tissue perfectly able to contract.
The grades matter, because they are separate problems sharing a name.
In first degree block every impulse gets through, only late: the atrial to ventricular interval stretches past two hundred milliseconds.
In the second degree pattern known as Wenckebach, that interval lengthens with each beat until one impulse fails and a beat is dropped.
Both usually sit in the node itself, both turn up in healthy people, particularly in athletes at rest and in almost anyone asleep, and neither alone is a reason to act.
Most blocks are a finding, not a disease.
The dangerous ones look different.
In the second degree pattern called Mobitz type II, beats drop without warning, which places the fault below the node, in the His and Purkinje wiring, where tissue tends to fail further.
In complete block nothing crosses.

The atria carry on at their own pace while the ventricles fall back on whatever escape rhythm they can raise, often only twenty to forty beats a minute, prone to pausing long enough that the person faints where they stand.
That is the problem the artificial pacemaker was built to solve.
Nineteenth century investigators had driven an animal heart at any rate they chose, and by the early 1930s a physician had built a hand cranked device he called an artificial pacemaker.
Practical machines arrived in the 1950s, and they worked, which was the remarkable part.
They were also brutal.
Pacing ran through electrodes on the chest wall, so the current crossed skin and muscle, with burns and pain severe enough that patients were sedated.
The units were the size of a cabinet on wheels and ran on wall current.
Wall current was the flaw that broke the design open.
In 1957 a power failure cut electricity to a hospital where children were being paced, and a surgeon asked a local repairman to build something independent of the grid.
The answer was a battery powered box small enough to wear, wired through the chest wall to the heart.
The first fully implanted unit went into a patient in Stockholm in 1958.
It failed within hours and a second within days.
The limit was now chemical.
Those units ran on zinc and mercuric oxide cells that gave twelve to twenty four months of service and vented hydrogen gas as they discharged, so the case could not be sealed.
Body fluid crept in and shorted the circuits.
Two answers were tried.
One was nuclear: a pellet of plutonium warm from its own decay driving a thermoelectric converter, which lasted decades but carried a regulatory burden.
The other, introduced in 1972, was the lithium iodine cell, which used a solid electrolyte, produced no gas, and could therefore be sealed inside a welded titanium can.
Within a decade the unit could sense the patient's own beats and hold its pulse, be reprogrammed through the skin, and report on its own condition.
Here the story takes an unexpected turn.
The generator, the part that looked hard, became the reliable part: batteries now announce their decline months ahead.
The stubborn problem turned out to be the lead, the insulated wire running from the can through a vein into the heart, the one component that has never stopped failing.
A lead must flex with every heartbeat, on the order of one hundred thousand times a day and forty million times a year.
Conductors fracture, classically where the lead is pinched between collarbone and first rib, and insulation cracks.
The tip has troubles of its own.
A pacing pulse counts only if it is strong enough to capture, meaning that it actually provokes a contraction rather than fading at the electrode, and the energy needed is not fixed.
Scar tissue forms around a fresh tip over the first weeks and drives the requirement up.
The fixes were small and elegant.
Tips shrank to a few square millimeters, concentrating the same current into a higher density, and the metal was made to release a steroid slowly into the surrounding tissue.
Lower capture energy meant smaller pulses, and smaller pulses meant a longer battery.
Taking an old lead out is harder than putting a new one in.
The tissue reaction that anchors the tip also binds the lead to the vein wall, and after a few years the wire is no longer a separate object.
Locking stylets and cutting sheaths exist for the job, but the vein the lead has fused to tears easily.
This is much of why self contained capsules, with no wire leaving the heart, have drawn such interest, and equally why enthusiasm for them has stayed measured rather than triumphant.
A device with no lead cannot suffer a lead fracture.
It will still have to come out someday.
A dual chamber pacemaker senses activity in the atrium, waits, and then paces the ventricle, and the wait is programmable, usually between about one hundred twenty and two hundred milliseconds.

Engineers spent five decades building a machine that could reproduce, in titanium and software, the tenth of a second that a knot of unremarkable tissue on the floor of the right atrium has been giving away for nothing.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Purkinje fibers in the ventricular walls reach threshold on their own at a rate of about
choices: sixty to one hundred times a minute
one hundred twenty to two hundred times a minute
forty to sixty times a minute
twenty to forty times a minute
three hundred times a minute

proof.quote: The Purkinje fibers in the ventricular walls are slower still, twenty to forty.

questions.why: Paragraph 4 lists the pacemaker sites in order from fastest to slowest, and the Purkinje fibers come last at twenty to forty times a minute.
distractorNotes: That is the sinoatrial node's rate, given first in the same list.
Those numbers are the programmable waiting interval in paragraph 18, which is measured in milliseconds rather than beats.
That is the rate of the atrioventricular junction, the middle member of the list.
Three hundred a minute is the atrial rate in flutter from paragraph 7, not any pacemaker site's own pace.

questions.stem: The passage explains that conduction through the atrioventricular node is slow partly because
choices: its cells are joined by comparatively few of the channels that pass current between cells
its cells cannot reach threshold on their own and must wait to be driven from above
a ring of fibrous tissue runs through the middle of the node and blocks part of the current
its cells depend on the same fast inward sodium rush that drives ordinary working muscle
the wave has to cross the whole of both atria before any part of it arrives there

proof.quote: joined by comparatively few of the protein channels that pass current from cell to cell

questions.why: Paragraph 6 gives three built in reasons for the delay: the cells are thin, they are joined by comparatively few of the channels that pass current from cell to cell, and their upstroke depends on calcium.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 says the atrioventricular junction reaches threshold on its own at forty to sixty a minute, so this reverses the passage.
The fibrous ring in paragraph 5 surrounds the route and leaves one door through it, and the passage never places it inside the node.
Paragraph 6 says the opposite, that the upstroke there depends on calcium rather than on the fast sodium rush.
That spread across the atria is described in paragraph 5, but it happens before the node and is not offered as a reason the node itself is slow.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the zinc and mercuric oxide cells in the earliest implanted units created a design problem because they
choices: could not deliver enough current to trigger a contraction of the chamber
gave off a gas as they discharged, so the case could not be sealed
lost all of their remaining capacity suddenly and with no warning at all
needed a thermoelectric converter to turn their heat into usable current
could only be recharged by a coil held against the skin for hours

proof.quote: vented hydrogen gas as they discharged, so the case could not be sealed

questions.why: Paragraph 13 says those cells vented hydrogen gas as they discharged, which is why the case could not be sealed. Body fluid then crept in and shorted the circuits.
distractorNotes: Capture and the energy a pulse needs come up in paragraph 16, and the passage never blames the early cells for weak output.
Paragraph 13 describes those cells as short lived, twelve to twenty four months, rather than abrupt, and paragraph 15 says modern batteries give months of notice.
The thermoelectric converter belongs to the nuclear unit in paragraph 14, which was a different answer to the same problem.
Recharging never appears in the passage. Paragraph 14 mentions reprogramming through the skin, which is a different thing entirely.

questions.stem: The passage states that a pacing lead is flexed roughly
choices: one thousand times a day
one million times a day
forty million times a day
one hundred thousand times a year
one hundred thousand times a day

proof.quote: on the order of one hundred thousand times a day and forty million times a year

questions.why: Paragraph 15 gives both figures in one sentence, about one hundred thousand flexes a day and forty million a year. The daily figure is the one asked for here.
distractorNotes: That is far below the number given, and the passage ties the flexing to every single heartbeat.
No such figure appears, and a million beats a day is far beyond any rate the passage describes.
Forty million is the yearly figure from that same sentence, not the daily one.
This swaps the two units. One hundred thousand is the daily count in paragraph 15.

questions.stem: Which two changes to the electrode tip does the passage credit with lowering the energy a pulse needs?
choices: a welded titanium can and a solid electrolyte sealed inside it
a locking stylet and a sheath that cuts a path along the body of the lead
a larger tip surface and a stiffer, thicker conductor running to it
a much smaller tip and the slow release of a steroid into nearby tissue
an atrial sensor and a waiting interval the operator can program

proof.quote: Tips shrank to a few square millimeters
the metal was made to release a steroid slowly into the surrounding tissue

questions.why: Paragraph 16 names both fixes: tips shrank to a few square millimeters, which concentrates the same current into a higher density, and the metal was made to release a steroid slowly into the surrounding tissue.
distractorNotes: Those belong to the battery and its case in paragraph 14, which is a different part of the device.
Those are the lead extraction tools from paragraph 17 and have nothing to do with the energy a pulse needs.
Paragraph 16 says the tips got smaller rather than larger, precisely so the same current is concentrated into a higher density.
That describes the dual chamber timing in paragraph 18 rather than anything done to the tip.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 3, "leaky" most nearly means
choices: damaged in a way that allows charge to escape
unable to hold any voltage across the membrane at all
joined to neighboring cells by channels that stay open
steadily admitting a small inward current
liable to tear open under mechanical pressure

proof.quote: channels swing open that admit a slow trickle of positive charge

questions.why: Paragraph 3 uses the word for a membrane that admits a slow trickle of positive charge as soon as the cell reaches its most negative point. It is a normal working feature of these cells, not damage.
distractorNotes: The everyday sense of a leak is something escaping through a flaw, but in paragraph 3 the charge moves inward and nothing is broken.
The cell does hold a voltage. It simply will not hold still at one value, since it climbs toward threshold instead.
Channels between neighboring cells appear in paragraph 6, where their scarcity slows the node, and that is a separate idea.
This borrows the plumbing sense of a leak. Nothing in paragraph 3 involves pressure or tearing.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 16, "capture" most nearly means
choices: to record the chamber's electrical activity for later review
to hold the tip of the lead firmly against the chamber wall
to succeed in triggering a contraction
to soak up the energy of the pulse without responding to it
to take over pacing duty from the sinoatrial node permanently

proof.quote: meaning that it actually provokes a contraction rather than fading at the electrode

questions.why: Paragraph 16 defines the word right where it uses it: a pulse captures when it actually provokes a contraction rather than fading at the electrode.
distractorNotes: Recording is a fair everyday sense of the word, but the passage is describing a pulse the device sends out, not data it takes in.
Anchoring the tip is discussed in paragraph 17, where scar tissue binds the lead, and the word capture is never used for it.
This is the opposite of the passage's meaning, since a pulse that fades at the electrode is exactly one that failed to capture.
Taking over from the sinoatrial node describes an escape rhythm in paragraph 10, while capture in paragraph 16 refers to a single pulse.

questions.stem: Suppose the sinoatrial node in a particular heart slowed to about thirty impulses a minute. The passage most supports which expectation?
choices: The ventricles would stop entirely until the node recovered its usual speed.
The atrioventricular junction would be expected to set the rate instead.
The fibrous ring would begin to carry current from the atria downward.
The Purkinje fibers would speed up to about sixty impulses a minute.
The heart would by definition be in complete block from that moment on.

proof.quote: Since all of them are excitable, the fastest wins
The atrioventricular junction manages forty to sixty.
the slower sites wait underneath as backups

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says the fastest site wins and the slower sites wait underneath as backups. At thirty a minute the node is no longer fastest, so the junction, listed at forty to sixty, would reach threshold first.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 describes the slower sites as backups, which is exactly why a slowed node does not stop the heart.
Paragraph 5 says the fibrous ring carries no current, and nothing in the passage suggests that ever changes.
The rates in paragraph 4 are each site's own pace, and nothing lets a slower site run faster than its own.
Paragraph 10 defines complete block as nothing crossing from atria to ventricles, which is a failure to conduct rather than a slow node.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which statement about a person whose atria are firing about three hundred times a minute?
choices: The Purkinje network will turn away the extra impulses on its own.
The ventricles will follow every one of those impulses unless the atria are stopped.
The sinoatrial node will take control back as soon as the fibrous ring conducts.
Any degree of block at the node would make the situation more dangerous.
The ventricles are spared largely because the node passes only a fraction of them.

proof.quote: The node refuses on their behalf, passing only a fraction.
nothing in the ventricles is equipped to refuse

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says the ventricles cannot follow either of those atrial rhythms and survive, and that nothing in them is equipped to refuse, so the node refuses on their behalf and passes only a fraction.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 7 says nothing in the ventricles is equipped to refuse, which is why the node has to do the refusing.
This ignores the rationing in paragraph 7, which is precisely what keeps the ventricles from following the atria.
Paragraph 5 says the fibrous ring carries no current, and paragraph 7 gives the node no role in restoring a normal rhythm.
Paragraph 7 treats the node's habit of holding impulses back as protective here, so slowing at the node is the opposite of dangerous.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central point of the passage?
choices: Better battery chemistry is the single main reason implanted pacemakers eventually became practical devices.
Most conduction abnormalities that turn up on a tracing are harmless findings that call for no treatment of any kind.
The heart's own signal proved hard to imitate, and the effort to replace it kept relocating the hardest problem.
The atrioventricular node is the most fragile structure in the heart and the usual site of serious disease.
Self contained capsules placed inside the heart have now resolved the problems that every earlier design could not.

proof.quote: Every cardiac device ever built stands in for that internal source.
The stubborn problem turned out to be the lead
Engineers spent five decades building a machine that could reproduce

questions.why: The passage runs from how the heart makes and routes its own signal, through what happens when that routing fails, to the devices built to stand in, and it ends with the hard problem moving from the power source to the wire.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 14 does credit the lithium iodine cell, but paragraph 15 says the battery stopped being the hard part, so this covers only one stretch of the story.
Paragraph 9 makes that point about first degree block and Wenckebach, and paragraph 10 turns immediately to the blocks that do need a device.
Paragraph 7 treats the node's narrowness as a safety feature, and the passage never calls it the most fragile structure or the usual site of disease.
Paragraph 17 says enthusiasm for those capsules has stayed measured, and that a capsule will still have to come out someday.

questions.stem: Paragraph 7 is included mainly in order to
choices: show that a feature that looks like a weakness is also the system's best protection
introduce the grading of blocks that the next two paragraphs go on to lay out in detail
explain why a disorganized atrial rhythm has to be treated as a medical emergency
argue that the heart would be better served by a faster route through the fibrous ring
prepare the reader for the external devices of the 1950s and the trouble they caused

proof.quote: The most conspicuous bottleneck in the system is also its finest safety feature.
poor design for speed and excellent design for protection

questions.why: Paragraph 6 explains the delay in terms of filling. Paragraph 7 adds the second job, rationing, and closes by saying the most conspicuous bottleneck in the system is also its finest safety feature.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 8 does that work, and paragraph 7 is still describing the normal node rather than any block.
Flutter and fibrillation are mentioned only to show what the node protects against, and treatment of them never comes up.
This inverts the paragraph, which praises the narrow slow passage instead of wishing it were faster.
Those devices arrive in paragraph 11, and paragraph 7 gives no hint of the history that follows.

questions.stem: Which best describes how the passage is organized?
choices: It alternates between individual patient cases and the laboratory findings that stand behind each of them.
It lays out a natural system, how it fails, the devices built to replace it, and where the difficulty settled.
It states an argument at the very start and then spends the rest of its length answering objections raised to it.
It follows one strict chronology from the nineteenth century forward to the present day without any digression.
It compares two competing devices point by point and then recommends one of them over the other.

proof.quote: The signal behind each beat is manufactured inside the heart
When conduction along that route falters, clinicians call it a block
That is the problem the artificial pacemaker was built to solve.
Here the story takes an unexpected turn.

questions.why: The first half builds the natural conduction system and the blocks that interrupt it, the middle traces the devices built to replace it, and paragraphs 15 through 17 show the hard problem moving from the generator to the lead.
distractorNotes: No individual patient cases are presented anywhere in the passage.
The passage is explanatory rather than argumentative, and no objection is ever raised and then answered.
The history in paragraphs 11 through 14 is chronological, but the first ten paragraphs are not a history at all.
Only one kind of device is traced here, and the passage recommends nothing to anyone.

questions.stem: The author's treatment of the external pacing machines of the 1950s is best described as
choices: admiring of how elegant and comfortable they had become by then
dismissive of the physicians who were willing to use them on patients
candid about how crude they were while granting that they worked
neutral throughout, offering no evaluation of them in either direction
regretful that anyone attempted such a thing before better tools existed

proof.quote: they worked, which was the remarkable part
They were also brutal.

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says the machines worked and calls that the remarkable part, then in the next breath calls them brutal and describes burns, sedation, and a cabinet on wheels.
distractorNotes: The paragraph describes burns, pain, sedation and a unit the size of a cabinet, none of which reads as elegant.
No criticism is aimed at the people using the machines. The judgment falls on the machines themselves.
Words like brutal and remarkable are plain evaluations, so the paragraph is anything but neutral.
The passage treats these machines as a real step forward, and paragraph 12 builds directly on them.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward self contained capsules placed inside the heart is best described as
choices: confident that they remove the last serious weakness left in the system
dismissive of them as a novelty with no real advantage to offer anyone
openly doubtful that they can pace a chamber reliably at all
interested while holding back full endorsement
worried that they will make lead extraction a far more common operation

proof.quote: enthusiasm for them has stayed measured rather than triumphant

questions.why: Paragraph 17 explains why the capsules are attractive, since a device with no lead cannot suffer a lead fracture, and then notes that enthusiasm has stayed measured rather than triumphant and that the capsule will still have to come out someday.
distractorNotes: The closing lines of paragraph 17 pull back from exactly that confidence by raising the question of retrieval.
The paragraph says the capsules have drawn such interest, which is not dismissal, and it names a genuine advantage.
Pacing reliability is never questioned. The reservation on offer is about getting the device out later.
The passage suggests the opposite, since a capsule has no lead at all to be extracted.

questions.stem: The passage supports each of the following statements EXCEPT:
choices: The sinoatrial node leads because it reaches threshold first, not because of any special standing.
A dropped beat can show up in a person with a perfectly healthy heart.
A ventricular escape rhythm is as steady and dependable as the node it replaces.
A cell with a solid electrolyte made a fully sealed pacemaker case possible.
A pacing lead has to bend with every beat for as long as it stays in place.

proof.quote: The node leads by speed alone, not by rank
one impulse fails and a beat is dropped
both turn up in healthy people
could therefore be sealed inside a welded titanium can
A lead must flex with every heartbeat
prone to pausing long enough that the person faints where they stand

questions.why: Paragraph 10 calls the escape rhythm slow, often only twenty to forty a minute, and prone to pausing long enough that the person faints, which is the opposite of dependable. The other four statements come from paragraphs 4, 9, 14 and 15.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 says the node leads by speed alone and not by rank, so this one is supported.
Paragraph 9 says the Wenckebach pattern, in which a beat is dropped, turns up in healthy people, so this one is supported.
Paragraph 14 credits the solid electrolyte of the lithium iodine cell with allowing a welded titanium can, so this one is supported.
Paragraph 15 gives the flexing figures for a lead, about one hundred thousand times a day, so this one is supported.

questions.stem: A reader who wants to know why the ventricles begin contracting near the bottom of the heart rather than at the top should look in
choices: paragraph 3
paragraph 5
paragraph 7
paragraph 10
paragraph 16

proof.quote: hands it to ventricular muscle near the apex
The ventricles therefore contract from the bottom upward

questions.why: Paragraph 5 traces the signal past the bundle of His and through the Purkinje network to ventricular muscle near the apex, which is why the squeeze runs from the bottom upward.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 3 is about how a single pacemaker cell drifts to threshold, not about where the wave travels.
Paragraph 7 is about the node holding back a flood of atrial impulses.
Paragraph 10 covers the dangerous blocks and the escape rhythms that follow them.
Paragraph 16 is about the electrode tip and the energy a pulse needs.
